assumptions: The alert firing at all is assumed to reflect a real error signal; this was not confirmed, and a spurious or mis-evaluated alert on a sub-second window has not been ruled out.
Customer impact is assumed to be minimal because of the very short open-to-close interval, but this is inference from the timestamps alone, not from any measurement of failed requests.
No remediation is assumed to have occurred, since no actions were recorded; the alert appears to have cleared on its own.
The absence of retrieved metrics is assumed to be a data-access or retention problem rather than evidence that the service emitted nothing; this was not verified.
input.executive_summary: An automated monitor raised an elevated-errors alert against one internal service. The alert opened and closed again almost immediately — the whole window was under a second — and the automated investigator was unable to read any monitoring data for that window, so how many requests actually failed, and whether any customer saw an error, is not known. No change was made to the service: the system acknowledged the alert, attempted an investigation, found no evidence to work from, and handed the incident to a person. Follow-up should focus on why monitoring data for the window was unavailable, since without it neither the cause nor the impact of this alert can be established.
input.root_cause: Not determined. The automated investigation could not retrieve any metrics for the incident window and no logs, traces, or remediation actions were recorded, so there is no evidence on which to base a cause for the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop. The only candidate the investigator produced was an explicit "no cause determined" placeholder, and the incident was escalated for human follow-up.
